name: Asymmetry of similarity
statement: The less prominent of two things is rated more similar to the more prominent than the reverse, so North Korea is judged more like China than China is like North Korea.
meaning: A similarity statement has a grammar. "a is like b" names a subject and a referent, and reversing them makes a different sentence. Tversky's claim is that the reversal changes the number a person gives when asked to rate the pair. His contrast model represents each object by a set of features and scores similarity from three quantities: the features the two share, the features of the subject that the referent lacks, and the features of the referent that the subject lacks. The two sets of distinctive features carry different weights, because attention settles on the subject of the comparison. Distinctive features of the subject then subtract more than distinctive features of the referent, and the object with more distinctive features loses more when it is the subject. Prominent objects have more features, so the prominent one should be the referent, and the pairing that puts it there should score higher. On that account symmetry survives in only two cases: when the two objects are equally salient, or when the question is put without a direction, as in "how similar are a and b to each other".

origin.note: "Features of similarity" set out the contrast model and reported the asymmetry experiments, which Tversky credits to a series run with Itamar Gati. The fuller write-up is their chapter "Studies of similarity" in Cognition and Categorization the following year, pages 79 to 98, and that chapter is what Many Labs 2 lists as the study it repeated. The two accounts describe the same country experiment and print the same test statistics.

evidence: The country study is the one everybody quotes. Twenty-one pairs were built so that one member was the more prominent, among them U.S.A. with Mexico, Belgium with Luxembourg and China with North Korea. A pretest asked a group to pick the more prominent country in each pair, and the 1977 paper puts that group at 69 people with agreement above two thirds for every pair but one. A second group of 69 chose which of two phrasings they preferred. They took the form that puts the prominent country second: 66 chose "North Korea is similar to Red China" and 3 chose the reverse, and across the 21 pairs the proportion choosing that form ran from 65.7 to 98.5 per cent. Then two groups of 77 rated all 21 pairs on a scale from 1, no similarity, to 20, maximal similarity, the groups differing only in the order of the countries inside each pair. Ratings were higher with the prominent country as referent. By pair, t(20) = 2.92, p < .01. Scoring each person by the average gap between the two orders gave a mean of .42, t(153) = 2.99, p < .01. Judgements of difference ran the other way, as the model predicts: two groups of 23 gave a by-pair t(20) = 2.72, p < .01, and a per-person mean of .63, t(45) = 2.24, p < .05. The claim was never confined to countries. Sixteen pairs of geometric figures, differing in goodness of form or in complexity, gave the same result on a 20-point scale, t(15) = 2.94, p < .01, with per-person means of .56 and t(131) = 2.96 and t(131) = 2.79 in the two sets. Tversky also took the prediction out of rating scales altogether. In a study with Yoav Cohen, 32 people saw pairs of block letters flashed on a noisy background and pressed a key for same or different. Where one letter contained the other, "same" responses came at 17.1 per cent when the contained letter was the variable and 12.4 per cent when it was the standard, t(31) = 4.41, p < .001. Reanalysing Rothkopf's 1957 Morse code data the same way, 336 of 555 comparisons between signals of unequal length ran in the predicted direction against 181 against, mean gap 3.3 per cent, t(554) = 9.17, p < .001. Wish's 1967 tone signals gave 241 against 117, mean gap 5.9 per cent, t(385) = 9.23, p < .001.

replication.headline: Many Labs 2 repeated the country study with 3,549 people and got an asymmetry of d = 0.01, and no sample in the project produced the effect in the original direction.
replication.detail: The country experiment ran as the twenty-eighth effect in Many Labs 2, on the second of its two slates, with the nation names brought up to date: Ceylon to Sri Lanka, West Germany to Germany, U.S.S.R. to Russia. Participants were split at random between rating similarities and rating differences, so each site contributed about half as much data to this test as to the other 27. In the similarities sample of 3,549, each person's asymmetry score was the average rating with the prominent country second minus the average with it first. That score sat at zero: t(3548) = 0.60, p = .55, d = 0.01, 95% CI [-0.02, 0.04], against an original of d = 0.48, 95% CI [0.16, 0.80]. The by-item analysis that mirrors Tversky's own came out backwards and flat, 9.42 against 9.43, t(20) = -0.29, p = .78, d = -0.04, 95% CI [-0.35, 0.26]. Table 2 records the tally across samples: 97.96 per cent non-significant, 2.04 per cent significant in the direction opposite the original, and none in the original direction. Heterogeneity was absent, Q = 15.33 on 48 degrees of freedom, p = .99, tau = .00, I squared 0 per cent. The difference ratings, on a separate 3,582 people, moved no further: t(3581) = 1.70, p = .09, d = 0.03. Table 5 puts the sample needed for 80 per cent power at the replication's own estimate at 313,958. This was not the first null. Aguilar and Medin ran three studies in 1999 aimed squarely at the rating asymmetry. Their Experiment 1 gave 84 undergraduates 12 country pairs and 12 animal pairs on a 1 to 9 scale, including five of Tversky's own country pairs, and found nothing: 5.48 against 5.39 for countries in the homogeneous condition and 5.48 against 5.52 in the heterogeneous one, with the animal means matching to within rounding. Naming the dimension of comparison out loud, as in "how similar is North Korea to China with respect to size", did not help. Experiment 2 used Tversky's own prominence measures and again found no rating asymmetry, though the prominence and feature-listing measures behaved as the contrast model says they should. Only Experiment 3, which showed each person both orders of the same pair back to back, produced ratings that differed, 4.22 against 3.97, t(11) = 2.30, p < .05, in 9 of 12 pairs. Their conclusion was that similarity rating asymmetries appear under quite circumscribed conditions.

study.cite: Klein, R. A., Vianello, M., Hasselman, F., et al. (2018). Many Labs 2: Investigating variation in replicability across samples and settings. Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(4), 443-490. Effect 28, Tversky and Gati (1978), Study 2.

replicated.weighting: global effect size pooled across all replication samples

limits: Many Labs 2 gives no per-effect count of contributing samples. Slate 2 was run by 61 of the project's 125 samples, and the heterogeneity test for this effect carries 48 degrees of freedom, which is as close to a lab count as the paper goes. Its description of the original also disagrees with the original. It puts Tversky and Gati's Study 2 at 144 participants, while both the 1977 paper and the 1978 chapter describe two groups of 77 and report t(153). The two Tversky accounts disagree with each other in smaller ways as well: the prominence pretest is 69 people in 1977 and 68 in the chapter, agreement is "all pairs except one" in 1977 and "in all cases" in the chapter, and the figures study is two groups of 67 in 1977 and two groups of 66 in the chapter, with identical statistics either way. What the replication found instead of an asymmetry was a procedural effect. One counterbalancing version of the list drew mean ratings of 8.78 and 8.84, the other 10.14 and 10.09, so which list a person received mattered and the direction of comparison did not. The test was of the country ratings alone. The block letters, the Morse code signals and the choice-of-phrasing result were not in the protocol, and no repeat of those was located here. Whether the contrast model is the best account of the original data is a separate question from whether the data hold. Krumhansl published a geometric alternative in Psychological Review in the same year as the chapter, arguing from spatial density rather than features; that paper is named here rather than weighed, because only its Crossref record was obtained. Aguilar and Medin's own reading is that prominence effects are real and that the link from prominence to rating asymmetry is the weak one. A different prediction from the same 1977 paper has been through preregistered replication with a similar outcome: Evers and Lakens reproduced Tversky's diagnosticity effect at 4.75 per cent on average, then found nothing left once substitution effects were ruled out. Searching for further replication attempts covered Crossref, PubMed, PubMed Central, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and open-web search in August 2026.
misreadings: The direction is the thing most often stated backwards. The less prominent item goes in the subject slot and gets the higher rating, so North Korea is judged more similar to China than China is to North Korea, and a toy train is more similar to a real train than a real train is to a toy train. Second, the measure is narrow. It is a number written on a 1 to 20 scale in answer to a directional sentence, and Many Labs 2 tested that and nothing else. Third, the phrasing result and the rating result are different findings with different fates. That people overwhelmingly prefer to say "North Korea is similar to Red China" is a large and lopsided effect, 66 against 3, and Aguilar and Medin found the preference measures held up while the ratings did not. Fourth, the original by-item pattern was never unanimous. Aguilar and Medin count Tversky's similarity asymmetry as holding for 15 of the 21 country pairs, close to the 9 of 12 they got themselves. Fifth, the failure here is a failure of an asymmetry in judged similarity, not a demonstration that similarity is a metric distance; the contrast model's other departures from geometry, and the confusion data, stand or fall separately. The idea is often filed with the other Tversky and Kahneman effects it does not belong to. It is not the representativeness heuristic, entry 145, which is about judging probability by resemblance rather than about resemblance itself, and it is not base-rate neglect, entry 37. The prominence of the referent is not the anchoring effect, entry 6, where a number rather than an object does the pulling. Nor is this the contrast effect, entry 197, which is about a judgement shifting away from a comparison rather than about which way the comparison points.
